Nigeria’s monetary policy rate could decline to an annual average of 21.7 per cent in 2027 and 18.6 per cent in 2028 as inflationary pressures ease, according to projections by Fitch Ratings. The forecast points to a gradual loosening of monetary policy over the next two years, although interest rates are expected to remain elevated as the country continues to battle high living costs and persistent inflation. Director of Sovereigns at Fitch Ratings, Gaimin Nonyane, presented the projections during the agency’s Nigeria Sovereign Rating Review and Outlook presentation on Tuesday. Fitch’s forecast shows that Nigeria’s average policy rate will fall from 27.3 per cent in 2025 to 25.4 per cent in 2026, before declining further to 21.7 per cent in 2027 and 18.6 per cent in 2028. The projections come amid signs of a gradual shift in the Central Bank of Nigeria’s monetary policy stance. In September 2026, the CBN reduced its Monetary Policy Rate by 350 basis points to 23 per cent from 26.5 per cent, marking its biggest rate cut since 2006. Fitch’s anticipated interest rate reductions are underpinned by expectations of a gradual decline in inflation. The ratings agency forecasts that year-end inflation will fall to 15.1 per cent in 2026 from 15.2 per cent in 2025, before dropping to 12.2 per cent in 2027 and 10.9 per cent in 2028. Nigeria’s headline inflation rate declined to 14.06 per cent in October 2026 from 14.63 per cent in September, marking the fifth consecutive month of moderation, although food inflation remained elevated at 19.13 per cent. Lessons from US midterms Nigerian T-bill yields fall to 17.79% as demand rises Easing inflation raises prospects of interest rate cut However, its average inflation forecast suggests that price pressures will remain significant in the near term, with inflation projected at 15.4 per cent in 2026 and 13.1 per cent in 2027. Fitch attributed the persistence of inflation to high food, transportation and utility costs, alongside elevated inflation expectations, although it expects easing services inflation to provide some relief. The agency also noted that the CBN’s restrictive monetary policy had helped slow credit expansion in the economy. Credit growth, which peaked at about 95 per cent in February 2024, had moderated to approximately 16 per cent by the time of the presentation. Fitch said the cash reserve requirement remained at 45 per cent, while excess liquidity in the banking system was expected to sustain tight monetary conditions through the remainder of 2026. It anticipates moderate monetary easing from 2027 as inflation gradually declines. On the broader economy, Fitch expects Nigeria’s gross domestic product to expand by 4.3 per cent in both 2026 and 2027, before slowing slightly to 4.2 per cent in 2028. The agency also projects the government’s fiscal deficit to widen to 3.6 per cent of GDP in 2026, before narrowing to 3.3 per cent in 2027 and 3.1 per cent in 2028. Nigeria’s foreign exchange reserves are expected to cover 6.3 months of current external payments in 2026, declining to 5.9 months in 2027 and 5.8 months in 2028. Fitch said recent economic reforms had improved the country’s policy credibility, external liquidity and ability to withstand economic shocks. Odinaka Anudu
